paper_title: Beyond Policy Rollouts: Embedding-Space Directional Exploration with Anchored Noise for LLM RLVR

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically uses small rollout groups per prompt, where repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, reducing within-group reward variation and weakening group-relative advantage signals. Existing remedies such as higher sampling temperature, entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping, and larger rollout budgets broaden sampling or modify policy updates but leave rollout conditioning unchanged. In this paper, we propose EDEN (Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise), which intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. EDEN explores beyond the policy's own rollouts. Within the same rollout budget, it replaces a small fraction of standard rollouts in each group with rollouts that the same policy generates from the prompt plus a single appended, perturbed embedding position, rather than from the prompt alone. Gaussian noise drives variation, while a shared anchor provides a common conditioning direction within each prompt group. Selected perturbed rollouts contribute to GRPO updates with downweighted advantages, and the model architecture, discrete decoding, and test-time inference remain unchanged. Across model scales and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EDEN outperforms GRPO and the exploration controls evaluated in the same pipeline, with the largest gains in sampled solution coverage. Analyses show that more prompt groups provide non-zero group-relative learning signals and that noise and anchoring play complementary roles. Intervening at the rollout source is thus an effective lever for exploration in RLVR.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the standard recipe for post-training reasoning LLMs, instantiated in algorithms such as PPO [21], RLOO [1], GRPO [22, 8], and DAPO [32]. Most of them share group-rollout backbone: for each prompt, the policy samples trajectories whose verifiable rewards drive the update, making rollout quality direct constraint on learning. Rollout generation is expensive, so typical training uses small groups of 816 rollouts per prompt. At this budget, repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, and the gradient sees narrow slice of the solution space [25]. The key constraint is therefore not rollout count alone, but the amount of useful variation within the rollout pool. This rollout homogeneity can cause the group-relative advantage signal that GRPO [22] relies on to collapse. When all rollouts in group receive the same reward, their advantages vanish, motivating dynamic-sampling filters in recent RLVR systems [32]. Over training, policy entropy can collapse within few hundred steps [6], and pass@k can flatten or even regress below the base model for large [33, 26, 30, 25]. These observations highlight exploration as shared bottleneck: the rollout pool needs more diversity than the converging policy alone can supply [40], making exploration central research focus in RLVR. Existing exploration methods for RLVR address this through different leverage points. Higher sampling temperatures [7, 36] broaden token-level sampling by flattening the output distribution, while entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping (Clip-Higher) [32], and entropy-collapse regularizers such as Clip-Cov / KL-Cov [6] aim to prevent premature concentration or relax policy updates. These methods encourage exploration by modifying the training objective or the sampling distribution, while leaving rollout conditioning unchanged. Other methods apply selection [17, 38, 32], pruning low-information trajectories or skipping groups with uniform rewards. distinct set of approaches directly alters rollout generation. Search-based methods branch from intermediate 1 states [27], whereas perturbation-based methods modify soft-token representations, policy parameters, and logits, or repurpose the noise inherent in quantised execution [3, 2, 13, 39]. These works suggest that the locus of exploration matters, since changing the conditions under which trajectories are generated can alter the effective trajectory distribution beyond simply drawing more rollouts from the same distribution. Can minimal input-embedding intervention enable useful trajectory-level exploration while retaining standard discrete decoding and leaving test-time inference unchanged? In this paper, we propose EDEN (Embeddingspace Directional Exploration via anchored Noise), an RLVR exploration method that intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. Without additional rollouts, EDEN explores beyond the policys own rollouts  (Fig. 1)  by conditioning the same policy on perturbed inputs for subset of each group, helping bring trajectories rarely obtained through standard sampling into training. Applied only during training, this conditioning is introduced at single embedding position immediately after the prompt and before the first generated token, allowing it to influence the entire autoregressive rollout from the outset without repeatedly intervening during decoding. EDEN therefore requires neither policy-parameter perturbations nor specialized decoding, and leaves test-time inference unchanged. The perturbation combines Gaussian noise, which allows rollouts to deviate from the standard generation mode, with an anchor embedding shared by all perturbed rollouts for prompt. The shared anchor provides directionality by defining common embedding-space conditioning vector for all perturbed rollouts of prompt, while independent isotropic Gaussian noise introduces local variation around it. To turn this additional exploration into useful training signals, EDEN retains perturbed trajectories with large absolute advantages and incorporates them into GRPO updates with downweighted advantages. Fig. 2 illustrates the training procedure. EDEN improves over GRPO across three model scales and also outperforms the exploration controls evaluated in the same pipeline. Mechanism analyses further support the effectiveness of input-side exploration. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Figure 1. EDEN explores beyond the policys rollouts. (a) Anchored conditioning yields rollouts from shifted proposal. (b) After training, EDEN achieves broader coverage of correct trajectories under clean-prompt sampling. (c) Independent Gaussian noise perturbs shared anchor in embedding space. We propose EDEN, new RLVR exploration method that intervenes at the rollout source through anchored noise: small fraction of rollouts are perturbed via anchored Gaussian noise, and the most informative perturbed rollouts are incorporated into training via an advantage-gated filter and noise-aware advantage reweighting. EDEN realises directional exploration through the complementary roles of noise and anchoring, with Gaussian noise driving variation and chosen anchor embedding supplying shared conditioning direction within each prompt group. The design integrates with GRPO through single appended embedding position, retains discrete decoding, and leaves the model architecture and inference unchanged. Across three model scales and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EDEN improves average Pass@1 and Pass@8 over GRPO, with its advantage persisting under Pass@256 evaluation on AIME. Training dynamics show more prompt groups with nonzero training signals, while controlled ablations support the complementary roles of noise and anchoring.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: RLVR and GRPO foundations. RLVR trains reasoning LLMs with verifiable rewards [16, 5], using algorithms such as PPO [21], RLOO [1], and GRPO [22, 8]. GRPO replaces PPOs learned value function with grouprelative advantage signal computed across rollouts sampled per prompt, and has become the dominant choice for verifiable-reward LLM post-training. DAPO [32] extends GRPO with asymmetric clipping (Clip-Higher), Dynamic 2 Sampling, token-level loss, and overlong reward shaping, which together stabilise large-scale training. Further variants refine advantage estimation, importance ratios, or training schedules while retaining the group-rollout backbone. Our work builds directly on GRPO and is compatible with these refinements. Exploration approaches in RLVR. Exploration is central challenge in RLVR, with policy concentration and limited solution coverage motivating range of approaches [33, 26, 30, 25]. Higher sampling temperatures [7, 36], entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping [32], and Clip-Cov / KL-Cov [6] broaden sampling or counter premature policy concentration. ProRL [18] extends training with KL resets to sustain exploration. Other methods reshape the optimisation objective itself. Pass-at-k Training [4], FlowRL [41], and Diversity-Aware Policy Optimization [31] adjust the reward objective to maintain diversity. These approaches modify sampling or optimization while leaving input conditioning unchanged. EDEN instead intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. Rollout methods for LLM RLVR. Some rollout methods improve efficiency by selecting informative rollouts or prompts, as in Dynamic Sampling [32], GRESO [38], CPPO [17], and related approaches [11, 20, 24, 19], or by reusing historical rollouts to amortise generation cost [12, 34, 37, 23]. Other methods promote exploration by intervening before or during generation. Tree search [27] branches from intermediate states to diversify trajectories. Soft Tokens [3] perturbs input embeddings at each CoT step with soft-token decoding, PSNGRPO [2] perturbs policy weights with truncated importance sampling, QeRL [13] exploits quantisation-induced noise, SofT-GRPO [39] applies Gumbel perturbations to logits with soft decoding, and REFT diversifies discrete first-token choices [14]. EDEN instead uses shared anchor to direct continuous perturbations at one appended input embedding for subset of rollouts.

sections.title: 3.2 Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise
sections.content: EDEN reshapes the rollout distribution through controlled embedding-space perturbations. It has three parts. Perturb samples fraction of each group from the same policy under perturbed input conditioning. Regulate controls exploration through shared vocabulary-token anchor, norm-relative noise scale, screened anchor bank, and temperature schedule. Absorb incorporates informative perturbed trajectories into updates of the unperturbed policy through advantage-based selection, advantage scaling, and evaluation under the clean prompt. 3 Figure 2. Overview of EDEN. EDEN augments RLVR with small fraction of noise-perturbed rollouts to broaden trajectory-level exploration without increasing the total rollout budget.

sections.title: 4.1 Main Results
sections.content: EDEN outperforms GRPO on average at both 1.5B and 7B scales across English and Chinese mathematics benchmarks from grade-school to olympiad level. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, we also compare with same-pipeline exploration controls, including Higher Temperature (T = 1.2) for increased sampling randomness and Clip Higher [32] for asymmetric PPO clipping. The entropy bonus and larger rollout groups are examined in Section 4.2. EDEN achieves the best average Pass@1 and Pass@8 in Table 1, exceeding GRPO by 2.44 and 3.06 points, respectively. Neither control alone yields comparable gains, highlighting the benefit of EDENs exploration strategy. The improvement persists at 7B  (Table 2)  . Across both scales, the larger gains on Pass@8 than Pass@1 are consistent with improved coverage of valid solutions under fixed sampling budget.

Breaking the Rollout Budget Ceiling simple alternative to EDENs structured perturbation is to increase GRPOs rollout budget, potentially providing more gradient signal and broader sampling. We compare GRPO with 8, 16, and 32 rollouts per prompt against EDEN with 16. Increasing GRPOs budget from 8 to 32 improves Pass@1 by only 0.5 points and slightly reduces Pass@8, whereas EDEN substantially outperforms GRPO at both matched and larger GRPO budgets  (Table 5)  . Fig. 5 shows that all GRPO configurations reach similarly low entropy by step 200, suggesting that sustaining exploration requires more than drawing additional samples from the same distribution. EDEN maintains higher entropy than every GRPO configuration after warm-up. Together, these results suggest that increasing GRPOs rollout count alone does not reproduce EDENs sustained exploration or performance gains. Role of Anchored Noise. Table 4 examines how noise, anchor choice, and anchor sharing affect EDEN. Removing noise reduces performance to the level of GRPO, showing that an unperturbed anchor alone is insufficient. Norm-matched random noise without an anchor also fails to reproduce EDENs gains. fixed random anchor recovers part of the improvement but remains below EDEN, showing that consistent anchoring can be useful even without bank diversity. Selecting new random anchor for every rollout performs worse, which is consistent with increased within-group dispersion when rollouts from the same prompt use different conditioning centers. EDEN instead shares one curated-bank anchor within each prompt group and samples anchors across groups, combining common within-group conditioning centre with variation across groups. Comparison with Exploration Controls We examine whether EDENs gains can be explained by conventional exploration controls applied during generation or policy updates. Increasing the entropy bonus on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B raises policy entropy throughout training without improving validation accuracy, which declines at larger bonuses  (Fig. 6)  . Higher sampling temperatures yield inconsistent gains, and extreme temperatures destabilize training under the default settings (Appendix E). Clip Higher [32] provides limited and inconsistent gains over GRPO, whereas EDEN achieves stronger performance with the same asymmetric clipping, supporting the benefit of its additional rollout-side intervention. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: RLVR faces limited exploration under small rollout budgets, with concentrated trajectories and weak learning signals. We propose EDEN, which explores beyond the policys own rollouts through directional input-embedding perturbations at the rollout source. It generates fraction of each group under perturbed conditioning and absorbs informative trajectories into the unperturbed policy through selective incorporation and advantage reweighting. This enables structured exploration without changing the model architecture, rollout budget, or test-time inference path. Across model scales and benchmarks, EDEN outperforms GRPO and the exploration controls in the same pipeline. These results suggest gains from input-side perturbations beyond output-side exploration controls alone. Limitations and Future Work. Several directions may further extend EDENs capabilities. First, the current noise bank is constructed from set of anchor embeddings. More adaptive or learnable constructions, such as dynamic selection or joint optimization with the policy, may enable more targeted exploration. Second, EDEN applies Gaussian perturbations centered at anchor embeddings. More structured schemes, such as anisotropic noise or task-dependent directions, may further improve coverage of the trajectory space.

sections.title: A Detailed Experimental Setup
sections.content: Datasets. We evaluate our method across diverse set of mathematical reasoning datasets, covering wide range of difficulty levels. For smaller models (Qwen2.5-0.5B), we train on the GSM8K training set and evaluate on both GSM8K and MATH. GSM8K focuses on grade-school arithmetic reasoning, while MATH contains more challenging competition-style problems. For math-specialized models (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B), we train on combination of the MATH training set and DAPO-Math, which together provide diverse and high-difficulty mathematical reasoning data. Evaluation is conducted on broad suite of benchmarks, including GSM8K and MATH (standard reasoning tasks), AMC, AIME 2024, and AIME 2025 (competition-level problems), as well as OlympiadBench, Gaokao, and MinervaMath, which further extend coverage to olympiad-style and advanced mathematical reasoning tasks. Models. We conduct experiments on three Qwen2.5 models spanning different scales: Qwen2.5-0.5B1, Qwen2.5Math-1.5B2, and Qwen2.5-Math-7B3. The Qwen2.5-0.5B model serves as general-purpose base model, while Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and Qwen2.5-Math7B are specialized for mathematical reasoning through domain-specific pretraining. This setup allows us to evaluate the effectiveness of our method across both general and math-specialized models, as well as across different model scales. Training Details. All experiments are implemented using the verl framework with vLLM for rollout generation. We use binary outcome reward that assigns 1 to correct responses and 0 otherwise. Across methods, the global batch size is 128 and the learning rate is 1 106. GRPO uses symmetric PPO clipping with ϵ = 0.2. EDEN and the Clip Higher baseline use asymmetric clipping with ϵlow = 0.2 and ϵhigh = 0.28. We set the KL coefficient to 0 and the entropy coefficient to 0.001. The maximum prompt and response lengths are 1536 and 2560 tokens, respectively. Qwen2.5-0.5B is trained for approximately 400 steps, corresponding to 6 epochs, while the math-specialized models are trained for approximately 2000 steps, corresponding to 10 epochs. All experiments are run on 8H100 GPUs. GRPO and EDEN use the same generation budget of 16 rollouts per prompt. GRPO generates all 16 rollouts from the unmodified input, whereas EDEN generates 12 standard rollouts and 4 noise-perturbed rollouts. For each prompt, EDEN samples one anchor from bank of 8 candidates and shares it across the 4 perturbed rollouts, while applying an independent Gaussian perturbation to the shared anchor for each rollout. We set the relative perturbation scale ρ to 0.12 for Qwen2.5-0.5B and 0.18 for the math-specialized models. For GRPO and EDEN, standard rollouts use fixed sampling temperature of τr = 1.0. The temperature for noise-perturbed rollouts follows cosine schedule from 0.2 to 1.0 over the first 250 training steps for Qwen2.5-0.5B, 200 steps for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, and 400 steps for Qwen2.5-Math-7B, and remains at 1.0 thereafter. Rewards and group-relative advantages are computed jointly over all 16 rollouts for each prompt. All standard rollouts are retained for policy updates. We rank the perturbed rollouts globally across each prompt batch by absolute advantage and retain the top = 0.5 fraction, so the number retained for an individual prompt can range from 0 to Kn. The advantages of the retained perturbed rollouts are scaled by γ = 0.5. Anchor Assignment. Sharing one anchor across the perturbed rollouts of prompt keeps the conditioning direction fixed within the group, while independent Gaussian perturbations introduce local variation around that direction. The anchor is resampled for each prompt, exposing different rollout groups to different directions from the fixed bank. 1https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B 2https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B 3https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-7B

sections.title: E Extended Ablation Studies
sections.content: Effect of Temperature Schedule. We study the role of the cosine temperature schedule in EDEN by analyzing both its necessity and the effect of its duration. As shown in Fig. 12, removing the temperature schedule leads to unstable training. The gradient norm grows rapidly and eventually diverges, resulting in numerical instability (NaNs), while validation accuracy initially improves but subsequently collapses to zero. This demonstrates that gradually increasing the sampling temperature is essential for stabilizing noise-perturbed rollouts during early training. We further investigate the impact of the schedule duration by comparing cosine schedules of 0200 and 0400 steps. As shown in Fig. 13, both configurations achieve comparable performance across most benchmarks and consistently outperform the GRPO baseline under both Pass@1 (greedy) and Pass@8 (sampling) settings. While extending the schedule to 0400 steps yields slight improvements on more challenging tasks, the overall differences remain modest. These results indicate that temperature scheduling is necessary for stable optimization, while performance is relatively insensitive to the schedule duration. This suggests that the primary performance gains of EDEN stem from the proposed noise-based exploration mechanism rather than fine-tuned temperature scheduling. Effect of Extreme Temperature Sampling. We observe that increasing temperature alone does not lead to consistent improvements across benchmarks. While moderate temperature (e.g., = 1.2) can improve performance on certain tasks, the gains are unstable and vary significantly across benchmarks. At extreme temperature (T = 1.4), training becomes highly unstable under the default setting due to excessively large entropy and stochasticity. To enable meaningful comparison, we set the entropy coefficient to zero in both GRPO and EDEN, as the exploration induced by high temperature alone is already sufficient.
